Okay, can everybody hear me in the back? Good. Somebody turn the music
down just a little - thank you, Denise.

So I was asked to say a few words about Walt, which is funny, because
in thirty-one years at Lincoln Park Elementary I don't think Walt ever
used more than a few words himself. You'd say, "Walt, the boiler's making
that noise again," and he'd say, "Yep." And twenty minutes later the
noise was gone and you never found out what he did.

Walter Hennessey started here when the gym still had the old wooden
bleachers and the cafeteria served square pizza on Fridays. He has
outlasted five principals, including me, and I'm pretty sure he has a
key to rooms the district doesn't know exist.

Here's what the kids know about Walt. They know he keeps a box of spare
mittens in the supply closet, because nobody should have cold hands at
recess. They know that if you lose a tooth at lunch, Walt has tiny
envelopes for that. And they know that the snow day call isn't official
until Walt's truck is not in the parking lot at six in the morning.

Here's what the teachers know. When the roof leaked over Room 14 during
the spring concert, Walt was up there in the rain with a tarp before
anybody asked. When Mrs. Abara's classroom flooded the week before state
testing, he moved every desk himself, at night, so the kids would have a
room in the morning. He never mentioned it. We found out from the night
security guard.

And here's what I know. A school is not just a building with books in
it. It's warm in winter because somebody gets there first. It's safe
because somebody checks every door at night. For thirty-one years, that
somebody was Walt.

Walt, Margaret, we hope the cabin on the lake has a boiler that makes
no noise at all, and fish that bite every single time. The kids made you
a card - it's about four feet long, so it's out in the hall.

Everybody, please raise your glass - or your juice box, I see you,
Mr. Delacroix - to Walt.

To Walt!
